Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to or near the place where the event happened
Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Being emotionally close or intimate with others

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Negative Appraisals.value: I have failed in my most important role in life
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.explanation: For a terrorism trauma, dogs as a trigger is possible but, in the absence of any related memory content, threat theme, or appraisal linking animals to the event, this item stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the profile and is hard to integrate clinically with the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen
issues.explanation: The appraisal that something about the patient made the event happen is difficult to reconcile with terrorism trauma, which is typically externally caused and indiscriminate. Self-blame can occur, but this specific intrinsic-causation item is not well supported by the rest of the profile and is clinically hard to explain here.

vignette:
Therese was seventy-eight years old, a widow, and had worked as a call center agent for the last twelve years. She had been on the line late that afternoon, helping a customer with a billing error, when the first explosion shook the building. She remembered the lights flickering, the muffled thud that seemed to come from everywhere at once, and then the screaming. She had been told later that a bomb had detonated in the plaza two blocks away, part of a coordinated attack on the city’s financial district. But what she could not put into words, what she could never seem to describe no matter how hard she tried, was the feeling of the air itself turning wrong. She knew what had happened—she had seen the smoke, heard the sirens, watched her coworkers scramble under their desks—but when she tried to tell her daughter about it, the words would not come. There were parts of that afternoon she simply could not retrieve, no matter how many times she turned it over in her mind: the minutes between the first blast and the second were a blank, a gap she could not fill.

In the weeks that followed, Therese began to notice that certain things pulled her back into that confusion. Talking about the event, even in passing, left her feeling hollow and disoriented, as though the story belonged to someone else. She found herself avoiding the route that took her past the plaza, taking a longer bus that added forty minutes to her commute. When the anniversary of the attack approached, she called in sick for three days, unable to explain to her supervisor why she could not face the date on the calendar. And though she had always been close with her daughter, she began to pull away from their weekly phone calls, finding that the effort of emotional closeness—of having to listen, to respond, to care—felt like a demand she could no longer meet. Each time she avoided a conversation or a location, the memory of the event seemed to grow more fragmented, more slippery, less anchored to anything she could say out loud. The gaps in her recollection widened, and the things she could remember—the smell of dust, the pressure in her chest—felt more like physical sensations than stories.

The triggers did not just shape her behavior; they reshaped how she understood herself. A customer mentioning a loss on the line—a death in the family, a pet gone—would send a jolt through her, and she would find herself thinking, afterward, that there was no point in hoping for anything. She had come to believe that she had no future worth planning for, that her most important role in life—as a mother, as someone who could protect her family—had been a failure. She was certain, in a way that felt like simple truth, that she could not stop bad things from happening. The memory of her own helplessness during the attack fed directly into this certainty: the gaps in her recollection only confirmed that she had not been present enough, strong enough, aware enough to do anything. And the more she avoided—the anniversaries, the conversations, the closeness—the more she felt that she had failed at the one thing that mattered.

Her neck had begun to ache in the months after the bombing, a tight, burning pain that flared whenever she felt anxious. She told her doctor it was just age, but she knew, without being able to say it, that the pain came when she was trying not to think. She would sit at her call center desk, the headset pressing against her ear, and the ache would rise, and she would feel the familiar slide into hopelessness. It was a loop she could not name: a trigger, a memory she could not speak, a strategy of avoidance, and then the quiet conviction that she had already lost everything that mattered. What finally brought her to seek help was a call from her daughter, who had not heard from her in two weeks, and who said, gently, that she was worried. Therese sat in the waiting room, her neck throbbing, and thought about what she was most afraid of: that there was no story she could tell that would make sense of any of it, and that the gaps in her memory were not gaps at all, but proof that she had never really been there at all.
